text.p: Mining contractor and civil engineer Macmahon Holdings Ltd is comfortable with forecasts of a 30 percent rise in net profit in 1996/97 to A$19.8 million, managing director Graham Biessel said in an interview.

"Subject to nothing falling off the truck, and particularly no extended wet weather in Western Australia, we will give that a good shake," Biessel told Reuters. The Adelaide-based company recorded a net profit of A$15.7 million 1995/96 to June 30.

Biessel said Macmahon was currently trading ahead of this time last year but he noted the company always had a better first half. He said three contracts in Kimberley region of Western Australia had yet to resume work after a recent cyclone.

Macmahon's share price has risen firmly from 63 cents in January 1996 to A$1.12 on Monday following a major restructuring in 1994. Biessel said the company has about A$700 million of work in hand and is looking at a 1996/97 turnover of about A$440 million, up on last year's A$357 million.

Among divisions, underground contractor National Mine Management (NMM) was expected to contribute A$85 million, western surface mining and civil operations A$230 million, eastern region A$105 million and Malaysian operations A$20 million, he said.

Biessel said the company's medium term earnings growth would come through its Asian operations and Australian underground contracts, although its move on the eastern states had been slower than anticipated.

Malaysia, where production at the Kepong quarry near Kuala Lumpur is expected to rise from three to five million tonnes in calendar 1997, had been a hard road, but was expected to produce a profit this year and solid earnings in 1997/98, he said.
Macmahon's first sand plant in Indonesia was due to be operational by April and to break even in 1997/98.
Biessel said the country offered good opportunities for contract mining work, particularly through Australian miners, in addition to construction materials supply, he said.
Biessel said that in the Australian market, while underground mining provided better margins, there was still room for growth in surface mining, tempered by intense competition.

"Whenever you are in a market place where there are five or six genuine competitors it is difficult, apart from the odd big project, to get any sort of a spurt in earnings growth," he said. "But the market itself, it still growing strongly despite various reservations people have got in terms of the gold price and native title issues," he said.

Biessel said he believed outsourcing now accounted for about 75 percent of Australian gold mining operations and the trend was growing. "We are certainly well down the path with iron ore. I think copper is well on the way and coal - probably the biggest market of the lot - is still in its infancy."
The potential coal outsourcing market could match the current A$2 billion value of the whole outsourcing industry if sensible labour market reform could be achieved, he said.
Biessel said BHP had signalled three or four major contracts to be called early this year "and we would like to think we would be able to get one of those at a sensible price."
Macmahon recently raised A$44 through a preferential share issue to fund debt and capital expenditure, estimated at A$100 million in 1996/97, and had cut its gearing ratio to 90 percent.

Biessel said he was quite comfortable with the gearing ratio in a business which required such major annual expenditure and believed investors and analysts should view the contracting sector's debt levels differently to manufacturers or miners. While acquisitions were still being pursued to assist NMM's move into the eastern states, Biessel said Macmahon was not pursuing a general major acquisition strategy, despite much talk of industry rationalisation driven by its growth prospects.
"I would prefer to try to grow the business organically," he said.
